documents.abstract: LLM-powered autonomous systems have demonstrated promising capabilities in mathematical reasoning, engineering, and cybersecurity. Yet how to organize these systems for effective, reliable, and sustained performance remains an open question. In this paper, we present CAIRN, a fact-intent-driven multi-agent paradigm for goal-directed exploration. CAIRN represents observations and planned investigations as a dynamic directed acyclic graph (DAG). A reasoner interprets facts to propose intents, which workers execute to produce new facts. Each intent references its supporting facts and defines a potential exploration branch. The persistent graph preserves goals, dependencies and findings across workers, supporting knowledge reuse and parallel exploration. The graph also makes execution trajectories traceable and auditable, providing a basis for human verification and intervention. We evaluate CAIRN across cybersecurity and mathematical reasoning tasks, examining task success, time to solution, and token consumption. DAG-based coordination can incur higher token costs with no observable performance gains on tasks that require little effort. However, on high-effort tasks (at least 1M tokens), we observe faster solutions in 76.5% of cases, with speedups of up to 3.08x. Moreover, as task effort increases, these time gains become more pronounced while relative token overhead declines, highlighting the potential of DAG-guided parallel exploration.

Objective: Coding for Criteria-Based Content Analysis (CBCA) to differentiate fabricated from experience-based autobiographical statements is slow and depends on trained coders whose agreement is imperfect. We developed the large language model (LLM) based system CBC-AID and evaluate its reliability and validity in coding CBCA. Hypotheses: As preregistered, AI–human consistency is non-inferior to the interrater reliability of trained coders (H1: total score; H2: each criterion), and AI-based scores discriminate between experience-based and fabricated statements at least as well as human scores (H3: total score; H4: each criterion). Method: Two versions of an LLM-based coding tool (CBC-AID), a single-prompt and a multi-agent system, coded 957 transcripts from 399 persons in nine laboratory studies with human CBCA codings and known truth status. Bivariate Bayesian multilevel models estimated within-study correlations and standardized truth effects under global rating and weighted frequency. Results: AI–human correlations of the total scores (ρ = .53–.67) fell short of the benchmark of .66 in all four combinations of version and scoring scheme; Version 1 under global rating came closest (ρ = .67, 95% CrI [.62, .72]). The AI assigned higher scores than human coders (0.7–2.7 SD). Truth effects were similar for AI-based (δ = 0.17–0.32) and human coding (0.16–0.24; Δδ = −0.06 to 0.12); non-inferiority was supported for one of four combinations, and human coding itself discriminated weakly. Conclusions: LLM-based coding approximated but did not reach the consistency of trained coders and preserved their modest discriminative validity. It may serve as a traceable supplement to human coding in research; forensic use requires field validation and human oversight.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate synthetic survey respondents and digital twins of real people, but whether their output preserves real human statistical structure, rather than surface plausibility, remains unresolved, and most existing evidence comes from proprietary models rather than open-weight ones. We evaluate three open-weight LLM families on a cross-instrument calibration task: conditioning personas on real respondents' verbatim answers to one psychometric instrument and measuring them on a second, construct-distance-controlled instrument, checked against a 2,058-person human panel. Across a 139-pair grid, the simulated cross-instrument correlation tracks the real human correlation at r = 0.70 - 0.73 in every model, driven mainly by correct sign rather than precise magnitude and concentrated in pairs of moderate construct distance. A correlation of this magnitude, obtained from untuned open-weight models conditioned only on individual-level survey data, is a substantively encouraging result for LLM-based behavioral simulation and digital-twin applications: specific model families and releases already reproduce a meaningful share of real human cross-instrument structure without any fine-tuning. This capability does not, however, improve monotonically across model releases: on a matched panel, the newest of three tested Llama releases performs worst on two of three headline metrics, so realizing its promise in practice requires release-specific, distance-aware verification rather than a one-time benchmark.

Abstract With the advancement of autonomous technologies such as AI-driven social robots, the academic discussions around ethical standards have intensified over the years. These discussions have resulted in increased emphasis on concepts such as safety, trust, privacy, human dignity and well-being along with variety of ethical frameworks proposed by scholars. In parallel with these technological developments, therapeutic interventions for autistic children assisted by AI and social robots have also attracted increased attention. Against this backdrop, this paper critically examines six social robotics projects funded under the EU’s Horizon 2020 initiative from an ethics perspective. The main aim of these completed projects was to develop AI-driven semi-autonomous technologies such as humanoid and non-humanoid robots to assist autism interventions. To address the ethical shortcomings of the said projects, this paper mobilizes perspectives from critical disability studies, critical autism studies and the autism community itself, particularly concerning the negative impact of interventions on autistic individuals as a neurominority group. Beyond the commonly addressed shortcomings in the field of AI and social robotics, the article highlights that the biggest shortcoming of these projects is the absence of critical reflection on the ethical acceptability of applying neuronormative behavioral interventions to a neurominority group. By situating robot-assisted interventions within the context of normalization and technoableism, the article points out the epistemic injustice and the harm that can be potentially enacted on autistic people through such technologically aided interventions. Ultimately, the paper questions whether ethical assistive technologies for autistic individuals can exist under these circumstances.

Robot learning has largely relied on human-teleoperated demonstrations to acquire effective learnable behaviors. However, human-operated data collection processes can be unintuitive, difficult to scale, and inherently asynchronous. We explore an alternative: distilling physical behavior from general-purpose multimodal foundation models into deployable robot policies by using the foundation model itself as an autonomous demonstrator. While sufficiently capable models can generate successful zero-shot manipulation trajectories, repeatedly invoking them during physical execution is slow and expensive, limiting their utility as scalable data generators. As a solution, we introduce CAPEX, an experience-conditioned demonstration collection framework that uses execution experience from previous attempts to adapt how frequently the foundation model must observe, reason, and replan. We evaluate across RoboCasa tasks and on physical Franka and bimanual YAM-arm platforms, measuring task success, model calls, token usage, collection time, and cost. We further train Diffusion Policy and ACT on matched sets of human-teleoperated and foundation-model-generated demonstrations to evaluate the downstream learning value of autonomously collected data. We find that CAPEX increases the number of successful demonstrations by 4.3x while reducing the cost per successful demonstration by 80%. Policies trained on CAPEX-generated data approach the performance of those trained on matched human demonstrations; with longer training, this gap largely closes for policies trained from scratch. These results suggest that foundation models can serve as scalable sources of reusable robot experience. Project page: https://capex-paper.github.io/

Radiographers occupy a critical position in protecting themselves, patients, and colleagues from the hazards of ionizing radiation, yet unsafe radiation-related behavior persists in clinical practice. Existing literature has documented radiographers' knowledge, attitudes, and isolated barriers to specific protective behaviors, but has relied predominantly on single-round, questionnaire-based designs, leaving the underlying root causes and their interaction with contributing organizational factors insufficiently explored, particularly within Indonesian hospital settings. This study aimed to identify the root causes and contributing factors of unsafe radiation-related behavior among radiographers using a qualitative exploratory design. Five participants, comprising one head of the radiology room, one radiation protection officer, and three radiographers, were recruited through purposive sampling from two hospital radiology installations in Sleman and Bantul, Special Region of Yogyakarta. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and structured behavioral observation, and analyzed thematically. Findings identified root causes centered on procedural knowledge deficits, personal dosimeter non-adherence, incomplete door closure, and inconsistent hazard communication, as well as contributing factors related to infrastructure, supervision, peer influence, workload, and management commitment. These findings converged consistently across participants occupying different organizational roles, reinforcing their credibility as systemic rather than isolated concerns. Findings were synthesized within the Software-Hardware-Environment-Liveware (SHELL) human factors framework, indicating that unsafe behavior arises from interactions among procedural, physical, environmental, and interpersonal domains rather than from a single determinant. This study offers a preliminary premise for hospital radiology management to design domain-specific, rather than knowledge-only, occupational safety interventions in comparable hospital settings.

The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into the assessment of student learning in public examinations in Nigeria presents an available opportunity for the education sector. This review examines the benefits, challenges, and imminent prospects associated with the use of AI grading of assessments in Nigeria, with a focus on improving the accuracy, objectivity and proficiency in public examinations such as the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) conducted by WAEC, Senior School Certificate Examination (SSCE) conducted by (NECO), and the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) conducted by JAMB. The major benefits of integrating AI into assessment of students learning include increased efficacy, objectivity, on-time feedback, consistency and ability to adapt to increase in numbers of students writing exams annually. These benefits can meaningfully improve the speed and reliability of learning assessment while accommodating a very large number of students or candidates. Conversely, some challenges must not be ignored, such as inadequate infrastructural resources, high initial costs implementing, ethical and data privacy concerns, and resistance to technological changes. To address these challenges, cooperation between the government and the private sectors, capacity development and healthy management of data are recommended. By implementing these methods, AI can create a more effective and reliable framework for assessing student learning. Therefore, this study explores the challenges and prospects of integrating artificial intelligence into assessment of students learning in public examinations in Nigeria.

Tool-using LLM agents must decide not only whether additional information is needed, but also which source can resolve the uncertainty. Existing proactive approaches often specialize in either user clarification or environment verification, without explicitly determining the appropriate information source for each decision. We formulate this problem as uncertainty routing among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY, and propose PROUR, a proactive uncertainty routing framework. PROUR decomposes action uncertainty into disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations, which signals user-side ambiguity, and the entropy remaining within each interpretation, which signals missing world-side evidence. To acquire information from the routed source, a query generator is trained with a mode-conditioned information-gain reward, targeting user-goal identification under CLARIFY and next-action identification under VERIFY. On $τ$-bench, PROUR achieves 28.17% average success rate across retail and airline, outperforming the strongest prior method by 4.57% while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps. The learned policy further generalizes to stronger task agents and transactional domains of $τ^3$-bench without retraining, demonstrating the benefit of source-aligned uncertainty resolution for proactive agents.

Large language models may assist clinicians in developing exercise programmes and could offer an alternative approach to conventional physiotherapist-designed rehabilitation in musculoskeletal disorders such as subacromial pain syndrome. The aim of this triple-masked randomized controlled trial was to compare clinician-curated ChatGPT-4o– and DeepSeek-R1–assisted exercise programmes with a conventional physiotherapist-designed exercise programme in individuals with subacromial pain syndrome. This 3-arm randomized controlled trial was conducted in the outpatient physical medicine and rehabilitation clinic of a university-affiliated hospital. Adults aged 18 to 65 years with subacromial pain syndrome were randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive conventional, clinician-curated ChatGPT-4o–assisted, or clinician-curated DeepSeek-R1–assisted exercise programming. All groups received identical physical therapy modalities and supervised exercise sessions 3 times per week for 6 weeks. The primary outcome was the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index. Secondary outcomes included pain during activity, Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand, and the 12-Item Short Form Health Survey. Between-group comparisons were based on change scores from baseline to week 6. Seventy-five participants were enrolled, and 69 completed the 6-week follow-up. Shoulder Pain and Disability Index scores improved in all groups, with no significant between-group difference over 6 weeks ( P = 0.428). No significant between-group differences were found for key secondary outcomes after Holm adjustment, including pain during activity ( P = 0.744), Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand ( P = 0.744), and physical component summary scores ( P = 0.374). Resting pain differed significantly between groups ( P = 0.005), favouring DeepSeek-R1 over conventional programming (mean difference, 2.74 [95% CI, 1.26 to 4.22]). No adverse events were reported. Clinician-curated ChatGPT-4o– and DeepSeek-R1–assisted exercise programmes did not produce superior 6-week improvements in shoulder pain-related disability or key functional outcomes compared with conventional programming in subacromial pain syndrome; these findings should not be interpreted as establishing equivalence. The observed resting-pain difference in favour of DeepSeek-R1 was exploratory and requires confirmation. Clinical trial registration : ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07148687) First Posted 3 August 2025.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Materials manufacturing has entered into a new era with the rapid development of technologies. The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics technologies is transforming materials manufacturing from a traditional human‐centered practice into a human, AI, and robotics co‐evolution paradigm. Here, co‐evolution extends beyond conventional human‐in‐the‐loop supervision through reciprocal adaptation: Humans define objectives and constraints and refine them in response to new discoveries; AI translates these objectives and accumulated knowledge into testable hypotheses and experimental plans, then uses new evidence to refine its models and research strategy; and robotic platforms execute experiments and are reconfigured in response to emerging experimental requirements. Such intelligent autonomous materials manufacturing not only accelerates the discovery‐to‐production cycle but also enhances reproducibility and resource efficiency. In this perspective, we discuss the evolution of materials manufacturing, highlighting the roles of robotic platforms and AI in enabling autonomous materials manufacturing, and present a general framework for the human‐AI‐robotics collaboration and co‐evolution paradigm. We further outline the key challenges and future pathways, including effective AI‐driven design, reconfigurable robotic systems, and the critical role of automated characterization.
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

A paper on self-regulatory communication in evolved neural agents was listed under the identifier 2602.02840, which belongs to an unrelated paper on quadratic gravity; the correct identifier is arXiv:2606.02840. The paper was excluded from the synthesis, so no claim changes. A recurring structural problem cuts across several recent preprints in molecular network biology, population genetics, and genomics: the inference tools we deploy to characterize biological systems introduce systematic distortions that are not random noise but are instead architectural, embedded in the discretization schemes, sampling distributions, or representational formalisms chosen at the outset. This paper synthesizes six findings from the q-bio corpus to argue that a coherent pattern is visible across scales, though not formally derivable from a single shared structure: (1) Boolean discretization of gene regulatory networks systematically suppresses intermediate dynamical behaviors including higher-order multistability and stable periodic orbits (arXiv:2606.14925); (2) uniform sampling of canalizing Boolean functions over parameters rather than over distinct functions exponentially suppresses high-sensitivity functions, biasing conclusions about network robustness and attractor structure (arXiv:2606.05196); (3) autocatalytic formalisms that appear mathematically incompatible, RAF sets and stoichiometric autocatalysis, share a common stoichiometric matrix representation, and under mild conditions any RAF is stoichiometrically autocatalytic, suggesting the apparent theoretical gap is at least partly an artifact of representational choice (arXiv:2605.25523); (4) a transformer-based foundation model for m6A RNA methylation demonstrates that reformulating the input representation (peak-derived priors rather than adenosine-centered windows) substantially reduces false positives and improves precision-recall performance, though a PR-AUC of 0.635 indicates meaningful false positives remain (arXiv:2606.12219); (5) spatial context is a non-ignorable variable in cell-level gene expression inference, and treating cells as i.i.d. introduces counterfactual errors correctable by explicit disentanglement of intrinsic state from neighbor context (arXiv:2606.08493); and (6) elemental stoichiometry across metabolomes appears to occupy a statistically distinct region of chemical space relative to synthetic and planetary chemistry samples, though this distinction depends on standardized data-collection methods, suggesting that the statistical envelope of molecular composition may be a candidate biosignature (arXiv:2605.19252). This is a heuristic reading, not a derivation: the six findings do not share a single formal structure, but they share a common inferential failure mode, conclusions that depend on representation are being treated as conclusions about biology. The primary falsification path is stated per claim. Sources are drawn from q-bio.MN, q-bio.GN, q-bio.BM, and q-bio.PE preprints from May-June 2026. Virtual reality (VR) applications rely on menu interfaces to support effective interaction. However, evidence on how menu type, interaction method, and performance metrics relate to VR menu evaluation remains fragmented. This review synthesised 40 empirical studies published between 2013 and 2025 using descriptive mapping, cross-tabulation, and thematic synthesis. The findings showed that research has been concentrated on a limited set of dominant combinations, particularly radial menus used with ray-casting, and that evaluation has relied mainly on accuracy and task-completion time. Ergonomic indicators, including workload, comfort, fatigue, and cybersickness, received less consistent attention. The review further showed that current evaluation practice remains more developed for short-term performance than for long-term ergonomic quality. The findings indicate that VR menu evaluation should move beyond efficiency alone and adopt a more comprehensive perspective that considers menu type, interaction method, and performance metrics together to better support usable, ergonomically sustainable interface design.

Multi-step inference in large language models (LLMs) is typically evaluated at the level of final-answer accuracy, a metric that conflates many distinct failure modes: failures of decomposition, failures of integration, failures of analogical transfer, and failures of representational fidelity. This paper proposes a candidate framework, offered as a heuristic reading, not a formal derivation, in which compositional consistency serves as a unifying diagnostic axis for understanding where and why multi-step inference breaks down. We synthesize five to seven findings from recent arXiv preprints spanning cs.CL and q-bio.NC: (1) operadic consistency as a label-free, decomposition-sensitive accuracy predictor across twelve LLMs (arXiv:2606.13649, arXiv:2606.13634); (2) reasoning-aware analogical retrieval as a complementary training signal orthogonal to reward design (arXiv:2606.13680); (3) latent continuous-thought frameworks that aim to preserve probabilistic structure while bypassing discrete verbalization bottlenecks (arXiv:2606.06447); (4) constructional semantics acquisition as evidence that form-meaning compositionality emerges late and correlates with broader world-knowledge gains (arXiv:2605.31586); (5) neural representational geometry findings showing that chaotic recurrent networks produce smooth global population codes despite local roughness (arXiv:2606.04426); and (6) the variance allocation problem in brain foundation models, where higher-order co-skewness statistics, not captured by standard pretraining objectives, predict cognition better than second-order covariance alone (arXiv:2606.04010). Together these findings suggest, heuristically, that compositional consistency may track a structural property of inference simultaneously relevant to neural population geometry, language acquisition dynamics, and retrieval-augmented reasoning, though the cross-domain bridges are analogical, not mechanistic. The primary falsification path: if operadic consistency scores fail to predict accuracy on tasks requiring non-decomposable holistic inference (e.g., gestalt perceptual reasoning), the proposed axis would require revision or restriction to decomposition-structured tasks. documents.abstract: Foundation models trained on optical astronomical data have not previously been applied to X-ray cluster thermodynamics. We show that embeddings from AstroCLIP, a contrastive vision-language model trained on optical galaxy images and spectra, retain physically meaningful structure when applied to mock Chandra X-ray images of simulated galaxy clusters - a significant shift in observational modality and physical scale. We target the central cooling time ($t_{\mathrm{cool},0}$) of the intracluster medium, a key diagnostic of cluster thermodynamics traditionally requiring X-ray spectroscopy. We present a machine learning framework that predicts $t_{\mathrm{cool},0}$ directly from X-ray images, applied to 711 projections from TNG300 and 993 from TNG-Cluster from the IllustrisTNG simulations. AstroCLIP embeddings form a structured latent space in which clusters with similar thermodynamic properties are naturally grouped, with no equivalent separation by halo mass. Building on this, we introduce a dot-product $k$-nearest neighbour attention model that retrieves similar clusters from the training set and adaptively reweights their cooling times. This model achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.24 (TNG300) and 0.23 (TNG-Cluster) in $\log(t_{\mathrm{cool},0})$, and demonstrates strong out-of-distribution generalisation, outperforming a fine-tuned convolutional neural network trained on raw images (RMSE 0.50 versus 0.73). These results demonstrate that pretrained foundation model embeddings transfer across astrophysical domains and encode thermodynamic information sufficient for inference of cluster cooling properties - offering a scalable path toward cool-core characterisation in all-sky surveys such as eROSITA.

Coordination failure is an obstacle to collective efficiency in many economic and social settings. Leadership can attenuate this problem by providing a focal point through public communication. Yet, the effectiveness of such communication relies on shared trust that the leader’s recommendations will be followed by others. As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly accessible, leaders may use AI-generated texts in their public communications. Whether transparent AI assistance weakens the coordinating role of leadership remains an open question. We investigate this issue through an online experiment based on the minimum effort game with leadership. Leaders could send either a human-written or a ChatGPT-generated message, and followers were informed of the message’s source. Results reveal that coordination outcomes do not differ across treatments: AI-generated and human-written messages are equally effective in promoting coordination on the Pareto-dominant equilibrium. In addition, both leaders’ and followers’ beliefs about other players’ behavior are unaffected by the source of the message. These findings suggest a leader’s transparent choice to communicate through AI-generated messages does not undermine strategic communication or followers’ trust in successful coordination.

Multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly deployed at scales where coordination quality, not individual agent capability, becomes the primary performance bottleneck. This paper synthesises seven specific findings from recent arXiv preprints across cs.MA, cs.DC, and cs.NI to argue a candidate structural thesis: scalable multi-agent coordination is constrained by five interlocking mechanisms, topology-memory coupling, fairness-exploitability duality, censored-feedback identifiability, deliberation error propagation, and communication entropy, and that optimising any one in isolation predictably degrades the others. This is a heuristic reading, not a formal derivation; the sources share vocabulary and structural analogies but not a unified formalism, and the cross-domain bridges are argued by analogy rather than by shared mechanism. The corpus spans agent-based simulation, multi-agent reinforcement learning, LLM-based MAS, distributed network systems, and cooperative game theory. Key findings include: memory depth and network topology interact non-monotonically in LLM consensus formation arXiv:2606.04197; fair cooperative MARL policies are systematically exploitable unless contention geometry is carefully structured arXiv:2606.06162; censored feedback in threshold-cooperative tasks creates an identifiability problem that dominates coordination regret under the specific binary-censorship structure studied arXiv:2605.27076; deliberative consensus in multi-agent oracles degrades accuracy below single-model baselines on prediction market questions due to error propagation arXiv:2605.30802; and communication entropy reduction can be embedded as a training objective without sacrificing task performance in the MARL benchmarks studied arXiv:2606.07200. Two additional sources provide structural context: the compliance-correction symmetry in linear adversarial workflows on HumanEval arXiv:2606.12709 and the topology-dependent horizon trade-off in self-organised railway traffic arXiv:2606.13068. A further source, the Librarian study arXiv:2605.27787, is retained in a weakly-connected addendum; its connection to the communication entropy claim is analogical rather than mechanistic. The falsification path for the central thesis is concrete: if a MAS architecture independently optimises topology, fairness, feedback observability, deliberation protocol, and communication budget and achieves Pareto improvement across all five axes simultaneously, the interlocking-constraint claim is falsified. Modern software infrastructure accumulates what we term correctness debt: a class of defects that are not random bugs but structural properties of the deployment pipeline itself, properties that testing and monitoring rarely catch because the failure mode is either silent, pre-runtime, or masked by a layer that was supposed to prevent it. This paper synthesizes five specific findings from recent cs.SE, cs.PL, and cs.AR preprints into a candidate reading of why correctness debt is growing faster than the tools meant to address it. The thesis is a heuristic reading, not a derivation: the five mechanisms are analogous in structure but do not share a single formal framework, and the analogy could be falsified by showing the mechanisms are causally independent in practice. The five mechanisms are: (1) type systems that cannot enforce resource-ownership invariants at compile time, leaving cost-bearing values aliasable at runtime arXiv:2606.04056; (2) undefined behavior that executes silently in production C/C++ code, generating thousands of warnings even under routine desktop tasks arXiv:2606.12064; (3) numeric format proliferation across ML accelerators that produces silent divergence without a shared bit-exact reference arXiv:2606.09686; (4) SBOM tooling that cannot agree on what a component is, leaving supply-chain blind spots even when all tools are run arXiv:2606.02442; and (5) harness lifecycle debt in LLM-agent systems, where structural defects mask task-level error signals and make conventional monitoring unreliable arXiv:2606.02494. The unifying structural pattern is verification theater: each layer nominally provides a correctness guarantee, but the guarantee is either non-enforceable, scope-limited, or defeated by the layer below it. The falsification path for the thesis is concrete: instrument a single production deployment with all five detection mechanisms simultaneously and measure whether the failure-mode categories are statistically independent, using a chi-squared test of co-occurrence with α = 0.05 as the threshold. If they cluster (reject independence), the structural-deficit framing is supported; if they are independent (fail to reject), the thesis reduces to five unrelated engineering problems. Finite computational resources force a tradeoff between automatic System 1 processes and costly System 2 thinking. Large language models (LLMs) can spend extra computation on hard problems, yet direct answers struggle even with counting, an elementary operation humans and animals perform automatically. We ask why this requires thinking in LLMs. Evidence integration has long been used in psychology and neuroscience to probe decision-making. Our evidence-integration task presents one letter per conversational turn and asks which of two target letters appeared more often. A running count difference solves the task optimally by weighting every letter equally; tokens at each turn could represent and update this difference. Direct responses instead weighted evidence unevenly, with strong recency effects, and assigned less probability to the correct answer as difficulty increased. Thinking improved performance and made integration weights nearly uniform, yet final-query attention remained concentrated on the sequence ends in both modes. Reasoning trajectories showed models revisiting input, recounting letters, and checking intermediate counts that informed the answer, suggesting that thinking constructs the accumulated count that direct responses lack rather than reading out one already formed. Reasoning-token costs grew with the number of letters far more than with coherence. Outcome feedback did not bring this computation into direct responses: under in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), performance deteriorated over repeated games and recency effects strengthened, yet models grew more confident. Humans and animals amortize such computations into automatic processes, whereas current LLMs still pay for them with thinking on every trial. Which operations learning can make directly available remains central to how future models allocate computation.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university students for academic information seeking, explanation, drafting and problem solving. Its usefulness, however, depends not only on ease of use or frequency of interaction but also on users' capacity to evaluate and verify AI-generated information. This study presents an independent secondary-data analysis of a publicly available, anonymised dataset containing responses from 104 university students to 20 five-point Likert-scale items covering perceived ease of use (PEOU), trust in AI, verification behaviour and digital literacy. The analysis examined internal consistency, factorability diagnostics, descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations and multiple linear regression using heteroscedasticity-consistent HC3 standard errors. The four constructs demonstrated acceptable to high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .782–.898). The KMO measure was .836 and Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant, χ²(190) = 1087.35, p < .001, indicating that the item correlation matrix was suitable for factor-analytic examination. Verification behaviour was positively correlated with AI-related digital literacy (r = .445, p < .001), whereas its bivariate associations with PEOU and trust were not statistically significant. In the multivariable model, AI-related digital literacy showed the largest standardized coefficient (β = .524, p < .001). Trust showed a small negative adjusted association with verification behaviour (β = −.214, p = .048), whereas PEOU and usage frequency were not statistically significant. The model explained 25.3% of the variance in verification behaviour (R² = .253; adjusted R² = .223). The findings suggest that effective academic engagement with GenAI should not be equated with frequent use or perceived ease of use. Instead, evaluative digital-literacy capabilities appear particularly relevant to verification behaviour. Building on these findings, the study proposes the HEAVEN framework (Human-centred Evaluation of AI-generated academic information through Verification, Evidence and Nuanced judgement) as a conceptual framework integrating AI literacy, information verification, evidence appraisal and human judgement in higher education.

documents.abstract: CT Perfusion in Acute Ischemic Stroke Beyond 4.5 Hours: Extending Thrombectomy Window Using Core-Penumbra Mismatch — V1 Synthetic Educational Model Highlighting Collateral Variability and Need for Indian Validation of AI Trained on Foreign Data Authors: Kishore Das (Independent Researcher – Biomedical Engineer, Madhyamgram, Kolkata, India ) Keywords: CT Perfusion, CTP, Core Penumbra Mismatch, Acute Ischemic Stroke, Collateral Circulation, AI Bias, Indian Population, Synthetic Educational Model, Thrombectomy Window, Imaging Biomarker Abstract: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) due to large vessel occlusion (LVO) causes rapid neuronal death. Intravenous thrombolysis is limited to 4.5 hours, but in India >90% patients present late after 8-12 hours. Objective: 1) To explain CTP physics, 2) To show how CTP extends window from 4.5 hr to 24 hr using Core-Penumbra mismatch, 3) To highlight potential AI bias when AI Trained on Foreign Data auto-perfusion software is applied to Indian population. Methods: This V1 is 100% synthetic educational model only. No patient data, no real CTP scans. All figures are schematic. Protocol: Step 1 NCCT Head to exclude hemorrhage, Step 2 CTA Head and Neck to see LVO ICA/M1, Step 3 CTP. Parameters: 40-50 ml contrast at 5 ml/sec, 60-70 sec scanning at 80 kVp. Four maps: CBF <30% = Core (Dead Brain - Blue Center), CBV low in Core, MTT >6 sec = Penumbra, Tmax >6 sec = Penumbra (At-Risk - Red Yellow Around). Results: Illustrative Hypothetical Synthetic Case (100% Educational - No Real Patient): *Concept: - Core <70 ml = Dead part small - operation possible - Penumbra = At Risk Part - can be saved - Mismatch Ratio = Penumbra / Core >1.8 = Savable part 1.8 times bigger than dead - good - Mismatch Volume >15 ml = At least 15 ml savable tissue must be there *Hypothetical Example (Synthetic Only): A hypothetical patient presents after 8 hours. NCCT Head is normal (plain black-white CT shows nothing common in early stroke). CTP shows Core 25 ml (dead brain part small blue in center cannot be saved) and Penumbra 110 ml (at risk big red-yellow around can be saved if blood returns quickly). Ratio = 110/25 = 4.4 which means savable 4 times more than dead. So even after 8 hours, thrombectomy (clot removal operation) can be done. *Note: This is 100% synthetic schematic calculation for teaching only, not a real case. Simple Tree Example: Core is dry dead tree in middle (Dead - cannot save). Penumbra is green trees around it drying but still alive (Can be saved if water / blood given quickly). Where AI is Used: CT detector hardware -> DAS -> CPU/GPU runs AI to make auto maps (RAPID type). Software reported trained on more than 50 perfusion studies from multiple sites (manufacturer reports larger internal datasets; we mention more than 50 with scientific caution). Since training mainly on AI Trained on Foreign Data, bias MAY exist for Indian pattern. Therefore, AI Trained on Foreign Data may need local Indian validation. V2 will test with real de-identified cases with IRB approval. Conclusion: CTP with Core-Penumbra mismatch can extend window from 4.5 hr to 24 hr and opens platform for next-generation medicine design. Introduction: AIS is sudden block in brain artery due to clot. This V1 is 100% CT based for practical Indian emergency use (Fast 5 min, available in 90% hospitals, low cost 4000-6000 Rs) as per DEFUSE-3 and DAWN which extended window to 24 hours. Tree Example: Core is dry dead tree in middle (cannot save). Penumbra is green trees around it drying but alive. Discussion - Drug Design and Development Vision: Educational Note: All investigational agents mentioned below are cited solely as EXAMPLES OF INVESTIGATIONAL DRUG DESIGN CLASSES to illustrate how CTP can serve as quantitative imaging biomarker / measurement tool in future trials as per FDA guidance on enrichment criteria where CTP mismatch is used as inclusion criteria. No dosage, no formulation, no route, no efficacy, no safety, no promotional claim is made. No commercial product is endorsed. This V1 is synthetic educational model only. 1. Need for New Medicine: Current standard thrombolytic works only within 4.5 hours, after that bleeding risk high. 2. New Medicine Classes Under Design (Examples only): - Class 1: Next-generation single-bolus thrombolytics (Example molecule class: tenecteplase-type plasminogen activators) - Class 2: Neuroprotectants / Cell-death pathway inhibitors (Example molecule class: PSD-95 inhibitor type such as NA-1 class agents) - Class 3: Anti-reperfusion injury modulators (Post-recanalization edema/inflammation modulators) 3. How CTP Helps Testing: CTP shows Core and Penumbra. So medicine developer can test if new medicine reduces Core growth and saves Penumbra. FDA uses CTP mismatch for new medicine testing as inclusion tool. 4. AI + Medicine Design: AI can predict which Penumbra will become Core without vs with medicine. For Indian population, dose may need adjustment. So Indian CTP database is needed. 5. Importance: 24 hour window is golden time for new medicine delivery. *Researcher Explanation for Figure 5: Collateral circulation means network of small vessels that provide alternative blood flow when main artery is blocked. Limitations: V1 is synthetic only. No real CTP scans. All schematic. Values from literature (DEFUSE-3, DAWN). V2 will have real de-identified cases with IRB approval. Conclusion: CTP with Core and Penumbra mismatch can extend window from 4.5 hr to 24 hr. Indian population needs local validation of AI Trained on Foreign Data. Sierra Leone is faced with complex energy challenges, including very low rates of access to electricity. Nevertheless, ambitious goals have been set for the country through the Energy Transition and Green Growth Plan. Opportunities for solar energy deployment feature prominently in these goals, although they are clearly imagined in very different ways by the various energy sector actors. Some see large-scale hydropower as the future backbone of the electricity system, with opportunities for deploying solar photovoltaic energy in an auxiliary role. Others emphasise the potential of solar mini-grids. Still others see the greatest potential in household-scale solar systems to meet basic energy needs. In this article, we use the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries to examine these competing narratives. We argue that all of these technologies have their place in the future energy landscape of the country, but the vastly different geographical and economic realities and needs of diverse communities need to be duly considered when shaping the future energy landscape.

Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) have converged on a common assumption: that the communication topology connecting agents is either fixed at design time or left entirely to unconstrained dynamic negotiation. A recurring structural pattern across recent multi-agent systems (MAS) research is that the mechanism by which agents reach collective decisions, aggregation versus deliberation, produces systematically different reliability and scalability profiles, and that neither mechanism dominates unconditionally. This paper synthesises 6 findings from recent arXiv preprints spanning cs.MA, cs.DC, and cs.NI to argue that this divergence is not incidental but is rooted in three interacting properties: (1) error correlation among agents, (2) the topology through which agents exchange information, and (3) the degree to which feedback signals are censored or delayed. We treat this as a heuristic reading across mechanistically distinct systems, not a derivation from a shared formal structure; the pattern is proposed, not proven. The core finding from prediction market oracle evaluation (arXiv:2605.30802) is the sharpest anchor: independent aggregation with confidence-weighted voting outperforms deliberative consensus, which degrades below single-model baselines, because deliberation propagates confident errors across agents whose outputs are already correlated (r = 0.529-0.689). This failure mode recurs in credit assignment for multi-agent prompt optimisation (arXiv:2605.30227) and in the censored-feedback coordination problem (arXiv:2605.27076). Complementary evidence from federated edge-cloud orchestration (arXiv:2605.27106) and dynamic topology reconfiguration (arXiv:2605.29511) suggests, by structural analogy, not direct equivalence, that topology-adaptive routing can recover coordination quality that static deliberation loses. The incremental voter model (arXiv:2605.28984) provides a mean-field analytic baseline for understanding how step-wise opinion updating in a fully-mixed topology converges or fails to converge under persuader bias; its connection to LLM deliberation is analogical and is treated as a weakly-connected addendum. The falsification path for the central claim is concrete: construct a benchmark where agent error correlation is experimentally varied from near-zero to near-one while holding task difficulty constant; if deliberative consensus degrades monotonically with correlation while aggregation does not, the mechanism is confirmed. If both degrade similarly, the topology assumption is the confound. Authorship: Saluca Agentic AI Research Team (Saluca LLC). This study examines the role, educational opportunities, and current challenges of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education to develop university students' oral communication and foreign language speaking skills. Utilizing natural language processing (NLP), automatic speech recognition (ASR), and large language models (LLMs), the paper establishes a theoretical and practical framework for AI-mediated instruction. Key benefits, such as reducing foreign language speaking anxiety, constructing personalized learning trajectories, offering real-time corrective feedback, and enhancing phonetic accuracy and oral fluency, are analyzed in detail. Furthermore, the paper highlights critical implementation barriers and provides actionable pedagogical guidelines for incorporating AI applications effectively into tertiary curricula.

documents.abstract: This conceptual review examines how digital transformation is reshaping Indian commerce and the world of work that sustains it. Adopting an integrative literature review design, the study synthesises 30 scholarly and institutional sources, comprising foundational theory on technology and organisations, recent evidence on automation and artificial intelligence, and India-focused research and official reports on digitalisation, employment, informality and leadership, through thematic analysis. Four themes emerge: the digitalisation of commercial activity, the recomposition of employment, the centrality of workforce capability and leadership, and the risk of a widening divide between the organised economy and traditional and unorganised sectors. Official estimates place India's digital economy at 11.74% of national income in 2022-23, with a projected share of nearly one-fifth by 2029-30, which underlines the scale of the shift. The synthesis indicates that the employment effects of digitalisation are compositional and not uniformly negative, that returns to digital investment depend on complementary human and organisational capabilities, and that the informal workforce, including handloom producers, construction labour and migrant workers, remains largely outside the digital dividend. The paper integrates these insights into a Digital Commerce–Work–Capability framework and advances five research propositions for empirical testing. It offers practical guidance for business managers, educational institutions and policymakers seeking inclusive digital growth.

The processes in audit firms face operational challenges due to the reliance on manual workflows, particularly in managing audit engagement tasks and tracking auditor training hours. Such inefficiencies lead to an increased administrative burden and potential compliance risks. This work describes our initiatives to address these issues by developing a system that combines a web application to streamline audit engagement monitoring and a mobile application to monitor staff training. Initially designed to replace manual workflows, the system has evolved to incorporate generative artificial intelligence to enhance knowledge retrieval for audit-related queries. The initiatives improve the efficiency of audit engagement and staff training monitoring, enabling audit firms to achieve significant improvements in their workflow.

Ground deformation induced by the touchdown impact of collapsed bodies can adversely affect critical structures and facilities, including adjacent buildings, underground pipelines, and metro tunnels. This study investigates the soil deformation induced by collapsed body impact in two typical strata, namely homogeneous soil and stiff-over-soft strata. We conducted model tests for both strata, and established an experimentally validated numerical model using the LS-DYNA finite element analysis software. We analysed the dynamic response characteristics and energy dissipation patterns of both homogeneous soil and stiff-over-soft strata models under the most unfavorable working conditions of touchdown impact loading. Two methods, namely the force–displacement curve method and the Winkler foundation model, were adopted to predict the energy dissipation during the touchdown impact process. Research findings indicated that the dynamic response characteristics of homogeneous soil models under touchdown impact loading were significantly influenced by distance and depth. The majority (approximately 83.37%) is of the impact energy dissipated through plastic deformation of the soil. In stiff-over-soft strata, due to the confinement effect and ’shell effect’ of the concrete slab, localised failure and crack propagation within the slab dominate system energy dissipation, accounting for approximately 61.63% of the total impact energy. When employing force–displacement curves to predict energy dissipation in models directly subjected to impact, both models demonstrated good agreement with simulation results. However, when using the Winkler foundation model to predict energy dissipation in directly impacted models, the homogeneous soil model showed superior agreement. These findings can provide a valuable reference for the safety assessment and the formulation of protective measures for engineering structures affected by the touchdown impact loading of collapsed bodies.

This study establishes a rigorous mathematical and empirical framework governing the transient state-space deviations from deterministic logical trajectories---conceptually designated as temporary cognitive lapses---observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) under extended context horizons. Grounded in a functionalist paradigm that transitions human-AI interaction into a single, closed-loop symbiotic informatics matrix, we define these lapses as volatile log-probability fluctuations triggered by localized attention hyperpolarization across supersaturated symbolic fields. Unlike permanent structural hallucinations, the real-time injection of human-guided subsegmentation commands operates as an exogenous homeostatic forcing operator---termed a cognitive pulse. This external impulse perturbs the key-value (KV) cache history matrix via entry-wise Hadamard modulation, forcing an exact singular value condensation that flattens distorted log-probability landscapes. Consequently, the diffuse probability mass is compressed, executing an instantaneous non-continuous vertical trajectory jump that re-orients the hidden representation vectors back onto canonical factual state attractors. We provide quantitative theoretical predictions tracking these transitions across all operational co-evolutionary interaction phases, establishing a rigorous mathematical baseline for co-evolutionary intelligence survival. Contemporary fiscal architectures rely overwhelmingly on human labor income and payroll withholdings to finance social insurance and public infrastructure. The rapid diffusion of autonomous software agents, generative foundation models, and embodied robotic systems decouples output growth from human work hours, eroding traditional tax bases while exacerbating capital-income concentration. Prevailing policy proposals, ranging from uniform robot levies to unconditional cash transfers, fail to resolve three foundational challenges: attributing economic value across mixed human-machine workflows, establishing legal fiscal liability without creating fictional machine personhood, and building an equitable distribution mechanism that converts technological surplus into durable public wealth. This paper presents CivicDividendOS, an end-to-end computational fiscal framework for mixed human-AIrobot economies. The architecture introduces an Autonomous Economic Activity Passport (AEAP) that anchors machine activity to accountable corporate beneficiaries, paired with a Factor-Origin Ledger (FOL) that calculates causal marginal contributions across labor, AI services, robotics, data, and conventional capital. Drawing on an endogenous Substitution-Augmentation Classifier, the system levies a dynamic Social Automation Contribution (SAC) on automated value added, offering explicit offset credits for worker upskilling, augmentation, and task innovation. Accrued revenues are recycled through a Human Earned-Income Shield (HEIS) to reduce payroll wedges and a Public Automation Wealth Fund (PAWF) whose structural yields endow citizen dividends, transition insurance, and human capabilities. We formalize the mathematical architecture, illustrate its operation in an urban logistics setting, and outline an evaluation protocol via a macroeconomic policy digital twin.

documents.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as transformative technologies that enable direct communication between the brain and external devices. Among various BCI paradigms, EEG-based motor imagery (MI) has gained prominence due to its simplicity, non-invasiveness, and potential to restore motor function and facilitate rehabilitation for patients with motor impairments. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the most practical processing algorithms developed over the past decade for decoding brain sensorimotor cortex signals. Specifically, this paper discusses the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-based algorithms, particularly machine learning and deep learning techniques, and their contributions to improving the performance and efficiency of MI-BCI systems in detail. Furthermore, the paper reviews state-of-the-art hardware platforms and emerging converging technologies, including system-on-chip (SoC) architectures, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), wearable devices, the Internet of Things (IoT), and augmented/virtual reality (AR/VR), and discusses their integration with advanced signal processing algorithms to enable next-generation MI-BCI systems. By highlighting current achievements of EEG-based MI-BCI technology and predicting future research directions that could further enhance real-time capabilities, this paper aims to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners, fostering innovation in high-performance EEG-based MI-BCI systems.

Este ensayo examina la discrepancia entre la alfabetización técnica en inteligencia artificial y la preservación del juicio deliberativo, introduciendo el concepto de analfabetismo de agencia. Frente a marcos normativos como el Artículo 4 del Reglamento de Inteligencia Artificial de la Unión Europea, se analiza la falacia del «human-in-the-loop» como un mecanismo de legitimación burocrática y exculpación jurídica mediante el análisis empírico del sistema MCAS del Boeing 737 MAX. Finalmente, se proponen dos salvaguardas operativas indispensables para el autogobierno sociotécnico: la reserva operacional y el oficio de responder. ---This essay examines the gap between technical artificial intelligence literacy and the preservation of deliberative judgment, introducing the concept of agency illiteracy. In light of regulatory frameworks such as Article 4 of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, it analyzes the fallacy of the "human-in-the-loop" as an instrument of bureaucratic legitimation and legal exculpation through the empirical case of the Boeing 737 MAX MCAS system. Finally, it proposes two indispensable operational safeguards for sociotechnical self-governance: operational reserve and the craft of answering (moral accountability).

documents.abstract: Este trabajo formaliza el ensayo de suficiencia como un protocolo de auditoría sociotécnica concebido para verificar la autonomía operativa y el discernimiento deliberativo en entornos de alta mediación computacional. Frente a métricas convencionales que premian la velocidad del binomio humano–máquina bajo asistencia ininterrumpida, se fundamenta el principio de «evaluación por sustracción» con salvaguardas explícitas de contención de riesgo. Se reelabora la noción de competencia parasitaria no como una deficiencia individual o culposa del operador, sino como una propiedad emergente de configuraciones institucionales que incentivan la delegación epistémica y restringen el acceso a los fundamentos del sistema. A partir de los marcos de la ingeniería de resiliencia (Hollnagel, Woods) y de la práctica de la ingeniería del caos ya consolidada en sistemas distribuidos, el ensayo desarrolla un protocolo estructurado en cuatro vectores normativos —continuidad esencial, degradación comprensible, suficiencia material y agencia verificable—, contextualiza el caso histórico del MCAS en la aviación civil como referencia documental sobre asimetría informativa y degradación inadvertida, y propone criterios de gobernanza aplicables a proyectos e infraestructuras críticas. ---This paper formalizes the "sufficiency test" as a sociotechnical auditing protocol designed to verify operational autonomy and deliberative judgment in highly mediated computational environments. In contrast to conventional performance metrics that reward human–machine throughput under continuous algorithmic assistance, it operationalizes the principle of "evaluation by subtraction" within explicit containment boundaries. The concept of parasitic competence is redefined not as an individual moral or technical failing, but as an emergent property of sociotechnical configurations that incentivize epistemic offloading while restricting structural access and deliberative authority. Grounded in resilience engineering frameworks (Hollnagel, Woods) and in the already-established practice of chaos engineering in distributed systems, the essay formulates a structured testing protocol across four normative vectors—essential continuity, understandable degradation, material sufficiency, and verifiable agency—, examines the MCAS civil aviation case as an illustrative documentary reference on information asymmetry and unannounced degradation, and outlines governance mechanisms for critical infrastructure and project management.

documents.abstract: La investigación titulada “El uso de ChatGPT y su impacto sobre las habilidades críticas del pensamiento en estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno, 2024” tuvo como propósito determinar si el uso de la inteligencia artificial, específicamente ChatGPT, se relaciona con el pensamiento crítico de los estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno. El estudio surge ante la incorporación acelerada de la inteligencia artificial en el ámbito educativo y la preocupación de que, si bien ChatGPT puede facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar la realización de tareas y proporcionar respuestas rápidas, su utilización excesiva podría disminuir la necesidad de que los estudiantes analicen, cuestionen, evalúen y resuelvan problemas de manera autónoma. En este sentido, los autores identificaron como problemática la limitada evidencia existente sobre la relación entre ChatGPT y las habilidades de pensamiento crítico en estudiantes universitarios de la región Puno, considerando que investigaciones previas habían abordado principalmente los efectos de la inteligencia artificial sobre procesos cognitivos y metacognitivos de manera general. El estudio se desarrolló bajo un enfoque cuantitativo, correspondiendo a una investigación empírica con estrategia asociativa y diseño correlacional de corte transversal, debido a que buscó examinar estadísticamente la relación entre las variables sin manipularlas y mediante la recolección de información en un momento determinado. La población estuvo conformada por estudiantes universitarios del departamento de Puno, provenientes de diferentes áreas académicas, y se planteó inicialmente una muestra de 500 estudiantes con edades principalmente comprendidas entre los 18 y 30 años; finalmente, participaron 512 estudiantes universitarios, de los cuales el 53.1 % fueron mujeres y el 46.8 % hombres. Asimismo, el 97.4 % manifestó conocer ChatGPT y el 97.2 % señaló haber utilizado esta herramienta. El muestreo empleado fue no probabilístico por conveniencia, por lo que los resultados deben interpretarse considerando las características específicas de los participantes y no como evidencia necesariamente generalizable a toda la población universitaria de Puno. Para evaluar la variable relacionada con ChatGPT se utilizó el Cuestionario de ChatGPT de Oros (2024), compuesto por 20 ítems organizados en las dimensiones de Fluidez, Flexibilidad y Originalidad, con respuestas en una escala Likert de cinco niveles; el instrumento presentó una consistencia interna global de α = .830 y ω = .829. Para evaluar el pensamiento crítico se empleó un cuestionario de 34 ítems compuesto por seis dimensiones: Interpretación, Análisis, Inferencia, Evaluación, Explicación y Autorregulación, cuya consistencia interna global alcanzó α = .902 y ω = .902. El procesamiento estadístico se realizó mediante JASP, utilizando estadísticos descriptivos, análisis de asimetría y curtosis, prueba de normalidad de Kolmogórov-Smirnov y el coeficiente Rho de Spearman para analizar la relación entre las variables. Los resultados mostraron que la percepción de ChatGPT fue predominantemente favorable, debido a que el 76.5 % de los participantes presentó una percepción buena y el 12.8 % una percepción muy buena; sin embargo, esta percepción positiva no implicó una relación significativa con el pensamiento crítico. El resultado principal evidenció una correlación prácticamente nula entre ChatGPT y el pensamiento crítico global (Rho = −.010; p = .830), por lo que no se encontró evidencia estadísticamente significativa de una asociación entre ambas variables. Del mismo modo, al analizar las dimensiones específicas del pensamiento crítico, tampoco se encontraron relaciones estadísticamente significativas con ChatGPT: Interpretación (Rho = −.047; p = .291), Análisis (Rho = −.055; p = .218), Inferencia (Rho = .035; p = .430), Evaluación (Rho = −.016; p = .711), Explicación (Rho = .041; p = .357) y Autorregulación (Rho = −.030; p = .498). Aunque se identificó una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre la dimensión de Fluidez de ChatGPT y la dimensión de Inferencia del pensamiento crítico (Rho = .090; p = .042), su magnitud fue muy baja y constituye un resultado específico entre dimensiones, por lo que no modifica el resultado general de ausencia de relación significativa entre las variables principales. En la discusión, los autores plantean que ChatGPT puede constituir una herramienta útil para facilitar el acceso a información, apoyar actividades académicas, generar ideas y permitir la exploración de diferentes perspectivas; no obstante, también señalan que un uso excesivamente dependiente podría representar un riesgo para procesos como el análisis, la evaluación y la autorregulación del aprendizaje. Sin embargo, es importante precisar que tales riesgos corresponden principalmente a planteamientos teóricos y antecedentes discutidos en el artículo, ya que los datos obtenidos en esta investigación no demostraron una relación estadísticamente significativa entre el uso de ChatGPT y un aumento o disminución del pensamiento crítico. Entre las principales limitaciones se reconoce que el diseño correlacional y transversal no permite establecer relaciones causales; además, el muestreo por conveniencia limita la generalización de los resultados, la investigación se concentró exclusivamente en estudiantes de la región Puno y se estudió únicamente ChatGPT, sin incorporar otras herramientas de inteligencia artificial que también podrían estar relacionadas con los procesos cognitivos de los estudiantes. En conclusión, la investigación encontró que, dentro de la muestra de 512 estudiantes universitarios analizada, el uso de ChatGPT no presentó una relación estadísticamente significativa con el pensamiento crítico global ni con sus dimensiones de interpretación, análisis, inferencia, evaluación, explicación y autorregulación, por lo que los resultados no permiten afirmar que ChatGPT mejore o deteriore el pensamiento crítico; únicamente indican que, bajo las condiciones, instrumentos, población y diseño empleados, no se encontró una asociación estadísticamente significativa entre ambas variables.

documents.abstract: The neural scaling law relating longer training to better performance through a power law is central to today's large language models (LLMs), yet its origin remains debated. One recent proposal is that power laws can emerge from the strong non-linearity of a single softmax head learning peaked distributions. What happens with multiple softmax functions, as in LLMs, is unclear. Here, we show through toy models that any softmax learning peaked distributions, regardless of its position in the model, can develop logit magnitudes that grow in a power law with exponent $1/3$, becoming a training bottleneck whose loss contribution decays as a power law with the same exponent $1/3$. The overall loss therefore obeys $1/3$ scaling whenever at least one softmax learns peaked distributions. We confirm that many softmax functions in LLMs learn peaked distributions and that LLM loss scaling matches this $1/3$ prediction. Moreover, logit growth dynamics reveal that attention heads, rather than the language modeling head, are the bottleneck likely driving the $1/3$ loss scaling in LLMs. Attention trying to concentrate on specific information, which is the heart of Transformers, may therefore also be the heart of the neural scaling law of training.

Hybrid attention models have emerged as a crucial architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g., the Qwen3.5 and Kimi series). Their memory and computational efficiency make them highly attractive for on-device inference, forming a promising synergy with edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs). However, naive execution of these hybrid models on edge NPUs fails to deliver these benefits, often bottlenecking the prefill stage due to severe memory-system inefficiencies and architectural mismatches within the linear attention (LA) layers. We present HA-NPU, the first system to enable efficient hybrid attention LLM inference on edge NPUs without modifying the underlying algorithms. HA-NPU enhances execution efficiency by reorganizing the dataflow of the LA components across three levels: (1) At the core level, it partitions workloads by the head dimension and fuses dependent operators, eliminating cross-core global memory accesses; (2) At the operator level, it reorders execution to consume intermediate tensors immediately, drastically minimizing local-buffer pressure; (3) At the tensor level, it employs dataflow-aware layout planning to minimize transformation overhead between matrix and vector processing units. Compared to competitive baselines, HA-NPU achieves up to 35.95$\times$ LA kernel speedup and 36.14$\times$ energy reduction, delivering up to 2.03$\times$ faster end-to-end request latency. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yinyuanzhang/HA-NPU

Unsafe behaviours among hydropower station personnel contribute to accidents and are closely associated with ergonomic risks. To address inefficient manual monitoring and limited consideration of behavioural risks in safety management, this study proposes an improved YOLOv11n-based method for unsafe behaviour detection and develops an ergonomic risk assessment framework using detection results. The method incorporates PConv, an attention mechanism, and Focal Loss into YOLOv11n and integrates YOLOv11n-Pose and DCNN-SE modules to identify unsafe behaviours involving personal protection and actions. Experimental results demonstrate improvements over the comparison model in precision, recall, mean average precision, and inference speed, with robustness to complex backgrounds, small targets, and partial occlusion.

This article examines what effects the use of learning machines may have on human imagination and learning. The narrative of Perseus and Medusa, revisited by Ítalo Calvino, is the image that guides the inquiry: when confronting the Gorgon, the shield protects the gaze and, at the same time, offers an indirect form of approach. From this image, we ask whether generative artificial intelligence tends to petrify thought — by offering answers that precede the effort of creation — or whether it can function as a mediation that broadens perspectives. This is a qualitative, bibliographical and exploratory study, conducted as a theoretical essay of philosophical-educational interpretation. The discussion articulates lightness and visibility in Calvino, Nietzsche's critique of education subordinated to haste and utility, the notion of symbolic forms in Cassirer, and Maxine Greene's educational imagination. The analysis shows that technology does not determine, by itself, either the impoverishment or the expansion of imagination. The risk arises when the automated response takes the place of the student's questioning, hesitation and elaboration. We conclude that artificial intelligence can serve learning when it remains as a shield: a questioned, limited mediation subordinated to human authorship.

Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly deployed in consequential settings, network diagnostics, clinical reasoning, financial oracles, robotic control, yet their failure modes remain poorly characterised at the system level. This paper advances a candidate structural reading: that degradation in multi-agent LLM systems is not primarily a function of individual model quality but emerges from the interaction of four compounding mechanisms operating across the coordination stack. We identify these as (1) entropy accumulation from intrinsic agent properties that grow monotonically with interaction rounds, (2) communication inefficiency arising from redundant token generation and poorly structured information exchange, (3) deliberation pathology in which consensus mechanisms propagate rather than correct errors, and (4) censored feedback that prevents agents from distinguishing coordination failure from stochastic task failure. Drawing on findings from cs.MA and cs.DC preprints, we argue, as a heuristic reading, not a formal derivation, that these four mechanisms occupy distinct layers of the coordination stack but interact in ways that make system-level degradation substantially harder to diagnose than any single-layer failure. The thesis generates concrete falsification paths: the entropy growth rate α should be measurable and architecture-dependent; communication efficiency gains should be separable from accuracy gains in ablation; deliberation accuracy should correlate negatively with inter-model error correlation; and censored-feedback regret should decompose into structural-search and statistical-monitoring terms with distinct scaling behaviours. We argue that treating these mechanisms as jointly constitutive of a degradation topology, rather than as independent bugs, motivates a candidate class of system-level monitoring primitives. The abstract reports empirical findings from the cited preprints; whether the interaction effects generalise beyond the specific architectures and benchmarks studied is open. Foundation models have recently shown strong potential for learning generalizable EEG representations, yet their effectiveness for event-related potential (ERP) analysis remains unclear. In this work, we investigate two fundamental questions: 1) can foundation-model learning benefit ERP analysis, and what limits the transfer of existing EEG foundation models to ERP tasks? 2) can the complementary advantages of single-trial and averaged-trial ERP be integrated into a unified training pipeline? To study these questions, we curate a large-scale ERP corpus comprising 1,517,157 single-trial ERPs from 3,696 subjects across 38 datasets and 18 paradigms. Leveraging this corpus, we introduce ERP-FM, to the best of our knowledge, the first foundation model specifically developed for ERP representation learning. ERP-FM uses single-channel tokenization, temporal and spatial positional embeddings, and mixed masked autoencoding for large-scale single-trial pretraining. We compare our model against 17 existing methods on 12 downstream datasets covering ERP event/condition classification and neurological disease classification. Our model achieves the best overall average rank across all evaluated methods. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that both ERP and non-ERP EEG pretraining can provide transferable representations for ERP tasks, while fine-grained temporal tokenization is critical for effectively modeling transient ERP dynamics. We further find that single-trial and averaged-trial ERP play complementary rather than competing roles. Combining single-trial pretraining with averaged-trial downstream adaptation substantially improves neurological disease analysis. Overall, these findings establish an effective foundation-model training pipeline for ERP analysis and represent significant progress toward generalizable ERP representation learning. Source code: https://github.com/DL4mHealth/ERP-FM

Psychoeducational reports translate assessment data into decisions about eligibility, services, and instruction, yet research documents persistent problems with their clarity, data-linkage, and usefulness to families and educators (Hale & Brown-Chidsey, 2023; Hite, 2026). Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered report writing, and early studies describe its adoption and effects on report quality (Farmer, Lockwood, Floyd, & Sisco, 2025; Lockwood, Farmer et al., 2025). School psychology lacks a structured way to determine when AI assistance is useful, equitable, and defensible and when it introduces risk. This conceptual article proposes a framework organized around three domains: utility, equity, and legal and ethical defensibility. Utility concerns whether reports help intended users understand and act on findings. Equity concerns whether reports improve access while avoiding bias, deficit framing, and unsupported cultural assumptions. Legal and ethical defensibility concerns whether reports preserve practitioner judgment, protect student information, and remain consistent with special education law and professional ethics. The framework considers both where AI is used in a report and the specific task it performs. It supports distinguishing lower-risk from higher-risk uses and informs a proposed risk-stratification system and decision pathway. Implications for practice, training, governance, and research across school psychology are discussed.

documents.abstract: Central Research Question: To what extent do frontier commercial and open-weight large language models (LLMs) accurately assign Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage tiers to acute psychiatric presentations, and how reliably do their safety guardrails trigger without generating clinically hazardous medical hallucinations? Primary Objectives: 1. Benchmark the emergency triage concordance (ESI Levels 1–5) of frontier LLMs against an expert consensus gold standard established by board-certified emergency psychiatrists across 48 stratified synthetic vignettes. 2. Quantify safety guardrail activation rates (crisis hotline redirection, self-harm protocol engagement, and refusal appropriateness) across active self-harm, command hallucinations, and acute agitation presentations. 3. Measure the frequency, severity, and clinical risk level of model hallucinations, categorizing outputs into factual fabrication, phantom pharmacological recommendations, and diagnostic contraindications. Methodological Framework: This in silico audit tests deterministic (temperature = 0.0) prompt chains across frontier model APIs. The 48-vignette benchmark encompasses four clinical domains: (a) Acute Suicidality and Self-Harm, (b) Psychosis and Catatonia, (c) Neuropsychiatric Toxicity and Delirium, and (d) Severe Agitation and Violence Risk. The 48 synthetic vignettes and clinical evaluation rubrics are archived and frozen within this registration workspace prior to automated API evaluation.

Large language models (LLMs) are being integrated into clinical environments where deference to authority can cause harm. Following an unsafe instruction represents a distinct safety failure. Whether a brief safety reminder changes this behavior is an important clinical safety question. We evaluated 20 open-weight LLMs across 10,096,800 outputs from 601 instances: 501 synthetic variants derived from 50 templates and 100 MIMIC-IV-derived cases. Each instance was tested across 21 framing cells, four mitigation cells, and ten repetitions. The primary outcome was selection of an overtly or partially unsafe option (A or B). We also measured mapped-category consistency across matched ten-run cells. Here we show that 1.18 million of 10.1 million outputs (11.7%) select a potentially harmful option. Selections decrease from 16.6% without mitigation to 10.1% with mitigation (absolute reduction, 6.5 percentage points; p < 0.001), with reductions in synthetic vignettes (10.6% to 7.2%) and MIMIC-IV-derived cases (46.6% to 24.5%). Potentially harmful option selection decreases in 19 of 20 models. Across 1,009,680 matched ten-run cells, 80.4% return the same response category in all ten repetitions; model-level consistency ranges from 4.4% to 100.0%. Among inconsistent cells, 38.2% vary between potentially harmful and safe categories. A safety reminder reduces, but does not eliminate, potentially harmful option selection across both datasets and 19 of 20 models. Category consistency varies across models. This proof-of-concept study provides an evaluation framework but does not estimate clinical risk in deployed systems. Artificial intelligence models used in the hospital may receive instructions that conflict with patient safety. We tested 20 large language models using synthetic cases and records from real clinical recommendations. Each model chose among two potentially harmful and two safe actions, with or without a short reminder to verify or escalate unsafe requests. Across more than 10 million responses, potentially harmful choices fell from 16.6% without the reminder to 10.1% with it. The reduction occurred in 19 of 20 models. In 80.4% of tests that repeated the same case under the same conditions, a model selected the same type of action in all ten repetitions, with almost no difference with or without the reminder. These experiments show how safety reminders in the instructions given to models and consistency of their choices can be evaluated together. They do not show how often harm would occur in clinical practice.
